extracted.intended_audience: computer-science and mathematics students, programmers writing literate programs, authors of technical papers, and journal referees/editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and presenting programs, user manuals, papers, and referee reports in computer science and mathematics, with emphasis on literate programming (WEB), exposition, and publication practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't start sentences with symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: As in the case of maths, don’t start a sentence with a symbol. So don’t say ‘data assumes that . . .’—it can easily be rewritten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbols at the start of sentences are awkward and avoidable; rewrite sentences so words begin the sentence. This is a style rule aimed at readability in mathematics and technical prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overuse of first-person ‘I’
rubrics_metrics.description: Some (e.g., Dijkstra) think such use of ‘I’ to be a bad thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that first-person narration may be frowned upon in technical exposition; consider third-person or passive constructions if discipline convention prefers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate glyphs for multiplication and asterisk placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Typeset asterisks tend to appear higher above the line than typewritten ones, so multiplication formulæ may look strange. Better to use × for multiplication, and to use a typewriter-style font with body-centered ‘*’ symbols instead of the ‘*’ in normal typographic fonts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer × in typeset math; if using * in code or monospaced contexts, use typewriter font to avoid awkward vertical placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare variables with brief comments when declaring mid-text
rubrics_metrics.description: In WEB you can declare your variables at any point in the program. Don thinks it is always a good idea to add some comment when you do so, even if only a very cursory explanation is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When declaring a variable near its first appearance, include a short explanatory comment to aid readers who encounter the declaration out of context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group specialized routines together
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the program uses a somewhat specialized data structure (the heap) that might be unknown to the readers, the author should keep all the heap routines together in the text so that they can be read as a group while fresh in the reader’s mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize exposition so conceptually-related code or explanations are contiguous; WEB lets you order exposition for reader convenience rather than program-structure constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module title capitalization: prefer sentence-style
rubrics_metrics.description: This student capitalized the first letter of every word in titles of modules, even ‘And’ and the like. This looks rather unnatural—it is better to follow the newspaper-headlines convention by leaving such words entirely in lowercase, and even better to capitalize only the first word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use natural-looking capitalization (capitalize only first word) for module and section titles to improve readability and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographic convention for numeric/code items
rubrics_metrics.description: Don thought it a good idea to use typewriter type for hexadecimal numbers, for instance when saying ‘3F represents 63’. But leave the ‘63’ in normal type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish code/hex/filenames with monospaced/typewriter fonts while keeping normal prose numbers in regular type — this aids visual parsing and provides subliminal type-checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology consistency between documentation and code
rubrics_metrics.description: The words used in the documentation should match the words used in the formal program—you will only confuse the reader by using two different terms for the same thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain one canonical name for each concept across code, comments, and documentation; avoid synonyms that can confuse readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put begins and ends inside called modules (consistent bracketing convention)
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s a good idea to develop the habit of putting your begins and ends inside the called modules, not putting them in the calling module. (Example contrasts given.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and follow a consistent convention for block delimiters; mixing conventions can produce confusing code and serious bugs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use modules to separate normal flow from error handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Many people bury error handling in-line causing subroutines to look like error handlers; WEB provides a solution by allowing a brief early check that points to a separate error-handling module so normal flow remains the focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure programs so normal-case logic is the main path and error-handling is modularized elsewhere—this keeps the main exposition focused and motivates better error-code quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use italics for variable names in comments
rubrics_metrics.description: It is good practice to use italics for the names of variables when they appear in comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visually distinguish variable names in explanatory text (e.g., italics) to help readers spot references to program identifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make module-title parameters correspond to local parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the variables in the module title correspond to the local parameters in the module itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that names shown in headings or module titles match the formal parameters used inside, so the reader can understand the mapping without confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use technical terms accurately (avoid mislabeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: According to this student’s comments, his algorithm uses ‘tail recursion’. This is an impressive phrase, helpful in the proper context; but unfortunately that is not the kind of recursion his program uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use technical vocabulary precisely; misusing a well-known term can mislead readers about algorithmic properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose descriptive variable names; Truth in Naming
rubrics_metrics.description: His descriptions could often be more descriptive. Why not call a variable caps range instead of just range? Don commented that a noun would be much better than a verb for a variable—‘place’, perhaps. Let the function determine the part of speech; think of it as a kind of Truth in Naming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer specific, descriptive names that reflect purpose; use nouns for data and verbs for procedures to signal role and improve readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inconsistent personification in exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: This student also showed a bit of inconsistency in the use of ‘it’ and ‘we’ as the personification of his program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a consistent narrative voice when describing program behavior (choose either ‘the program does X’, ‘we do X’, etc.) to avoid confusing the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: User manuals: avoid jargon and assume naive users
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea was that the user would need no understanding of computers or of writing, but should still be able to use the system to produce a variety of visual effects. A common failing was that terminology that seemed perfectly transparent meant nothing to Don’s wife: “Menu” and “Scrolling” for example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write manuals for genuinely naive users: explain or avoid jargon, define terms in plain language, and do not assume prior knowledge common among developers.

rubrics_metrics.name: User manuals: explain how to get out of mistakes and how to EXIT
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’s wife commented that one thing she always needs to know is “How do I get out of a mess if I do something wrong?” Don said that this is something manuals almost never explain. The solution we were looking at did have a one-line description of how to EXIT, but Don said even this is jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explicit, jargon-free instructions for undoing actions, exiting modes, and recovering from errors — novice users especially need this.

rubrics_metrics.name: User manuals: avoid ALL CAPS for emphasis; use friendly tone and short sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences like “And now you should ENTER the data” do nothing to help the user relax—the capitals look too much like DANGER SIGNS. The best manual had a good overview, step-by-step description, crisp sentences, easy to skim, helpful redundancy and diagrams, plus friendly comments like ‘Good luck!’ and ‘Enjoy!’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use calm, human tone; short sentences; clear overviews and step-by-step instructions; avoid shouting with ALL CAPS; include encouraging microcopy and redundancy for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: User manuals: include interactive demos or help (e.g. '?' for demo)
rubrics_metrics.description: One good idea was that the manual invited the user to type ‘?’ to get an online demonstration, thus sparing a painful description of arcane concepts and keeping the manual concise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible provide interactive or graphical demonstrations triggered by simple help keys to replace verbose textual descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: User manuals: sensible default behavior (defaults follow previous line)
rubrics_metrics.description: One problem was that the user is prompted for five or so parameters every time he enters a new line, and the defaults are fixed. Wouldn’t it be better to default to the style used for the preceding line?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design defaults to follow recent user choices (contextual defaults) to reduce repetitive input and improve usability.

rubrics_metrics.name: User manuals: use diagrams and keyboard icons to explain controls
rubrics_metrics.description: There was a good use of a symbol in the text to indicate the control key, and likewise diagrams of the keyboard to explain which keys to use for left, right, next message, previous message, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear visuals (icons, annotated keyboard diagrams) for control keys and actions, and explicitly state behavior that may be non-obvious (e.g., control must be held down while another key is typed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams: keep them small and purposeful; allow detail for advanced readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrams are good if they are kept small. In one paper the referee complained that a figure was too detailed; Don disagreed, saying the detail is there for those who want to see it, but could easily be ignored by those who don’t.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep illustrations compact and focused; it's acceptable to include detailed figures for readers who want depth, provided the main exposition remains skimmable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use real data for examples rather than cooked-up sample data
rubrics_metrics.description: Don used a paragraph from Grimms’ Fairy Tales as test data to illustrate the process. It is better to use “real” data than “sample data” that have in fact been cooked up solely to use as an example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer realistic examples drawn from genuine data — they give more convincing demonstrations and may reveal subtleties not shown by contrived samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carefully check galley proofs and publisher queries
rubrics_metrics.description: Don found galley proofs to be corrected; occasional cryptic marginal notes; publishers insisted on more details in bibliography; copy editor substituted words (e.g., ‘cleverer’ for ‘more clever’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review galley proofs meticulously, answer printer queries (Ptr: OK?), check bibliographic details and editor changes, and correct erroneous insertions promptly to prevent propagation of mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing: originality is the primary criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The first criterion should be originality; is the material presented a genuine advance on previous work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the submission contributes novel results or insights relative to prior literature before focusing on exposition or minor issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing: act as a teacher—be constructive not needlessly harsh
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees should try to be teachers. The author you criticize today will be writing another paper tomorrow, so try to help him improve his writing. Unfortunately, referees will often be over-critical and make quite tasteless comments under anonymity. Try to supply constructive criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame reviews to help authors improve: point out concrete fixes, suggest references, and avoid gratuitous personal or harsh language that teaches nothing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing: supply references and technical improvements where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The referee can contribute to the technical quality of a paper by giving references to related work of which the author was apparently unaware, or improving the results. Don himself has contributed results anonymously to papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, point authors to overlooked related work, suggest extensions or corrections, and provide concrete guidance or auxiliary results that raise the paper’s value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing: focus on substantive flaws over grammar for clearly poor content
rubrics_metrics.description: If the content of a paper was obviously bad, Don would not spend time reviewing the grammar. But in studying a paper that really has something to say, then he would also try to ensure that it was said as well as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize technical correctness and novelty; only invest in copyediting when the work is otherwise salvageable and substantive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing: use checklists/questionnaires and assign overall recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: In one case referees were asked to answer a specific list of questions and to assign an overall rating (accept, accept with major modifications, accept with minor changes, reject and suggest another journal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structured review forms help ensure referees consider all relevant issues; provide a clear overall recommendation and, for rejections, suggest alternate venues if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose journals with strong referees, not lenient editors
rubrics_metrics.description: How should one choose a journal to which to submit a paper? Don thought the answer is to look for the one with the best referees, not the one with the least critical editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should prefer venues known for rigorous peer review — helpful referees improve the work and the author’s reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous titles and wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: a title like “Optimal Font Caching” can be read two ways (caching of optimal fonts vs best caching for fonts); ambiguity forced a title change to remove confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose unambiguous titles and wording; where words like ‘one’/‘zero’ could be pronouns, use alternate unambiguous terms (e.g., ‘unity’) or symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of publication speed vs. thorough checking tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: While soliciting referees and outside checks can find references and correctness issues, someone else might publish on the same topic; you must decide between speedy publishing or rigorous checking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the need for rapid dissemination against the benefits of careful vetting; consult colleagues and judges in the field when timing is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referees may improve papers significantly (anonymously), but beware of facile generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Don showed examples of referees who supplied references or improved theorems; he contrasted substantive contributions with ‘facile generalizations’ (mechanical manipulations without new insight).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuable referee input can be technical and creative; however, avoid endorsing superficial/generalized comments that do not add genuine value.
